_fixture: Example content. Not the record. This file exists so tools/project.mjs and tools/browser-template.html can be built and checked before tools/read.mjs and the real node files land, and so every construct the page renders (arche root, mount shim, unstamped proposal, deferred ledger stubs, readings, an assumption, an unanswered question, a multi-parent node, cites, instruments, defined vocabulary) has at least one instance. Every question and answer below is invented.

public.about: the public part of the author's personal disposition, hosted here during bootstrap
public.liquidation: a repository answers at natb1.com with a `disposition` ref; public/ moves there and ids rewrite by prefix (ledger L03)

nodes.question: Who is the origin of what is done in my name?

instrument.ref: re-grasp on event, never on a calendar
instrument.note: The author reads the record after any event that could have moved authorship, and says whether they could still recover it.

nodes.answer:
I am. Delegation is expected and good: it buys attention at the level where intent is set. What must not atrophy is the capacity to notice that I have been captured and to recover, because an origin that cannot recover has been replaced.

This is an *archē*, a root: a starting point every other answer descends from, and the origin of the actions taken under them. It does not complete and it cannot fail.
nodes.rationale:
The modal content is the whole point. Capacity, not exercise. Being unable to recover is capture even when the delegate never misbehaves, and depending heavily on a tool you could drop tomorrow is not.

Written first because everything below it is a refinement of it, and because a root that arrives late is really a summary of decisions already made.

### Rejected

- *Detachment as the measure* — "how independent am I of the tool?" That measures the wrong thing. Dependence is fine; unrecoverable dependence is capture.
- *Forced detachment* — dogma, and dogma needs power to maintain.

nodes.question: Does the republican account of freedom as non-domination support this root?
nodes.source: Philip Pettit, Republicanism: A Theory of Freedom and Government (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1997), ch. 2, 'Liberty as Non-Domination', 51-79; with the restatement in On the People's Terms (Cambridge, 2012), ch. 1, sect. 1.2 on the eyeball test
nodes.answer:
Supports, and supplies the modal shape this root already has. Pettit's unfreedom is not interference but *domination*: standing exposed to another's arbitrary power, whether or not that power is ever used. A benevolent master still leaves a slave unfree.

**Adopted** directly. An AI that never once exceeded its scope, in a record that gave the author no way to check or withdraw, would still have replaced the origin.
nodes.rationale: Read during the bootstrap round on agency. Validated by the AI against its own knowledge of the text; the author has not read the loci yet, so the stamp is deferred.

nodes.question: What is this repository for?

instrument.note: The author reads this page and can say what the repository is for without opening anything else.

nodes.answer:
This repository exists so that a person can keep long-horizon AI work aligned with their explicit intent.

Two things live here. The **record**: a graph of questions and standing answers, each stamped with who decided it. The **instruments**: the small tools that read the record, project it for a person, and hand work to a session.

It is for one author and any number of AI sessions. It is not a framework, and it is not yet for anyone else to run.
nodes.rationale:
Why it matters leads up to the archē above. Delegating work to autonomous tools is expected; what must not be lost is the person's standing as the origin of what is done in their name.

Written as a target rather than a rule because it can be finished. There is a state in which the record is complete enough that a session never has to guess, and this answer names it.

### Rejected

- *Defining the repository by its parts.* The incumbent README describes a data structure plus a harness. That is scope, not purpose: it says what is here, not why.
- *Intent carried in prompts, chat, or memory.* Not durable, not reviewable, not rankable. It is the tacit form this repository exists to replace.
- *Issue trackers as the record of intent.* Tried here at length. They record work, not dispositions, and cannot carry authority or rank.

nodes.question: What is one record in this graph?

instrument.note: Every node file parses, carries exactly one question, and resolves every id it names.

nodes.answer:
One record is one **disposition**: a single question, and the answer that stands today.

Not a topic, not a component, not a strategy with a list of decisions inside it. If a text answers two questions, it is two records. If a new answer replaces an old one, the record holds the new answer and git holds the old.

A disposition is **ratified** when the author decided it, and the stamp names who and when. Everything else carries a weaker stamp, and the page says which.
nodes.rationale:
Scope is decided by the question, not by the size of the text. Two answers belong in one record only if they answer the same question, which is to say that one of them replaced the other.

Keeping history out of the record is what makes it readable: the current position is the whole file, and `git log` is the archive.

```
question:  one line, asked of the author
answer:    the position that stands
rationale: why, and what was rejected
authority: who decided, and when
```

### Rejected

Grouping by area (`publishing`, `dispatch`, `graph`). Areas are stable and questions are not, so an area node accumulates unrelated decisions until nobody can say what it holds.

nodes.question: How does a restatement hold a position that keeps changing?
nodes.source: American Law Institute, Restatement of the Law Third, Restitution and Unjust Enrichment (Philadelphia: ALI, 2011), Foreword and Reporter's Introductory Note; on the black-letter/comment/reporter's-note division
nodes.answer:
A restatement states the rule as it now stands, argues for it in comments, and puts the history in the reporter's notes, where it is available and out of the way.

**Adopted** directly: the answer field is the black-letter rule, the rationale is the comment, and git is the reporter's note.
nodes.rationale: The author named this form in the interview of 2026-09-02 and ratified it in the same turn, which is why the reading carries a ratified stamp rather than a deferred one.

nodes.question: Who may write which answer?
nodes.answer:
Three classes, and they attenuate downward.

- **ratified** — the author decided it. Only the author writes it.
- **delegated** — the author handed this class of decision to the AI and does not want to be asked again.
- **deferred** — the AI decided it inside the author's rules, and owes the author a review.

An answer the AI wants to give where it holds no authority is recorded as a **proposal**: inert, with no force, until the author rules on it.
nodes.rationale: Stubbed by the AI during bootstrap so that the pages below it have something to point at. The author has not read it, so it is stamped deferred and sits on the ledger until they do.

nodes.question: What does the tradition of practical wisdom say about deciding inside rules you did not write?
nodes.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.5 and VI.8, 1140a24 to 1142a30 (Bekker), trans. Terence Irwin, 2nd edn (Indianapolis: Hackett, 1999), read with Sarah Broadie, Ethics with Aristotle (Oxford, 1991), 179-198, on why phronēsis cannot be reduced to rule-following
nodes.answer:
Aristotle's *phronēsis* is the capacity to deliberate well about what conduces to living well, and it explicitly resists reduction to rules: the person of practical wisdom perceives what this particular situation calls for.

This record **diverges**. A session deliberates inside a scope it did not set, and the record — not the session's perception — decides where that scope ends. The divergence is deliberate: worse judgment at the edges, in exchange for an author who can predict what will happen while they are not watching.
nodes.rationale:
Recorded as diverged rather than adopted because adopting it would make the deferred class unbounded, which is the failure this graph exists to prevent.

Validated by the AI from its own knowledge of the loci. Deferred until the author reads them.

nodes.question: Which question gets read next?
nodes.answer:
**Rank**: one number per record, in `(0, 1]`, derived from where the record sits in the tree and from the author's boosts. It is never written by hand.

Rank is read three ways: the order to onboard in, the order attention flows in, and the floor below which a record is not loaded into a session. A **boost** is the author's own allocation, recorded when the hierarchy alone would give the wrong order.
nodes.rationale: The author has ratified that rank serves onboarding. The rest of this answer, including the three readings and the shape of the derivation, is the AI's and owes a review.

nodes.question: Should rank be computed from the citation graph rather than the hierarchy?
nodes.source: Page, Brin, Motwani and Winograd, 'The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web', Stanford InfoLab Technical Report 1999-66 (1999), sects. 2.1 to 2.5
nodes.answer:
The hierarchy was **chosen over** eigenvector centrality on the `cites` edges.

PageRank derives importance from what a corpus happens to point at, which is exactly the property that makes it robust for a web nobody authored. Here the corpus has one author, and importance is something they mean rather than something that emerges: a record cited often because it is awkward would outrank the root.
nodes.rationale: Kept as a reading rather than a rejected alternative in the rationale above, because it is a live tradition this graph may yet borrow from for the frontier ordering, where no author intent is available.

nodes.question: How does a newcomer read this record?

instrument.note: The page regenerates from the record alone, and from nothing else.

nodes.answer:
One page, generated from the record and nothing else, that opens on a single question and lets a reader walk from it to every other.

A **projection** shows the answer first, the reasoning under it, and the authority beside it. It never shows the file layout, and it never asks the reader to know what a commit is.
nodes.rationale:
Delegated: the author ruled that the shape of the projection is the AI's call, provided the record is its only input. A projection that needs a second source has become a document, and a document drifts.

### Rejected

Rendering the tree as a diagram first. A diagram shows the shape and hides the answers, and the answers are the reason to come.

nodes.question: Does this record have exactly one ratifying author?

instrument.note: No ratified stamp names anyone but the author.

nodes.answer:
Yes, and every rule above rests on it. One person stamps ratified; everyone else, including every AI session, writes at a weaker authority or writes a proposal.

If that stops being true — a second author, or a team — the answers above this one stop making sense and go back to the author rather than being patched.
nodes.rationale: Recorded as an assumption rather than a rule so that the record knows what to do when it fails. A rule that fails is a variance to be fixed; an assumption that fails sends the question above it back to the author, because the answer no longer means what it meant.

nodes.question: How is the bootstrap ledger disposed of?
nodes.proposal:
Each ledger entry is either ratified into a record or rejected, and the entry is struck as it goes. When the file is empty it is deleted, and its history stays in git.

The ledger is not part of the record: it holds bookkeeping for the bootstrap, and nothing in it survives as an answer. Entries still open are listed on the **Bootstrap** page beside the record that owes them.

This is the AI's candidate answer. It carries no authority, and the author has not ruled on it.
